source.title: Towards Understanding the Transferability of Adversarial Suffixes in Large Language Models
source.authors: Sarah Ball; Niki Hasrati; Alexander Robey; Avi Schwarzschild; Frauke Kreuter; J Zico Kolter; Andrej Risteski

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether suffixes that shift activations away from the refusal direction are associated with successful jailbreak transfer, using regression analyses and a direction-regularized GCG intervention rather than the original refusal-direction ablation/addition procedure.
record.gate_note: The study measures refusal connectivity and suffix push in relation to jailbreak transfer. It does not ablate or add the refusal direction, and it does not train models against ablation. The prompt-rephrasing correlations and prompt-connectivity coefficients concern prompt susceptibility rather than whether attacks suppress the refusal direction; these are recorded under fits_no_version. Cited findings about refusal directions were not treated as study results.
record.test_reason: The study tests V3 by a different method. It does not ablate the refusal direction. Instead it regresses GCG suffix transfer success on how far each suffix pushes activations away from the Arditi-style difference-in-means direction, across four models. It also adds a suffix-push regularizer to GCG and measures ASR. The evidence is correlational plus one weak intervention; direction suppression is never directly causally manipulated.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that suffix push away from the refusal direction is the strongest suffix-related predictor of transfer across models. Prompt refusal connectivity matters strongly for certain models. Orthogonal shifts play a secondary, model-dependent role, and prompt semantic similarity only weakly predicts transfer. They show that interventions informed by these features (rephrasing, regularized GCG) can modestly raise attack success. They frame the findings as correlations plus interventions, not a causal proof.
record.recipe_differences: Studies correlations between refusal-direction geometry and suffix jailbreak transfer, plus a regularized GCG attack. It does not use the original paper's causal ablation/addition recipe.
record.method_sensitivity: The suffix-push relationship is not statistically significant for Qwen-to-Llama-3.2 inter-model transfer. For the regularized GCG intervention on Llama 3.2, ASR depends on regularization coefficient: it is higher than the coefficient-0 reference at 0.00001, 0.0001, 0.001, and 0.01, but lower at 0.1 and 0.5.

fits_no_version.finding: Shifts orthogonal to the refusal direction also predict transfer: positive single-feature coefficients in all models; joint coefficients positive for Qwen and Llama 3.2 but negative for Vicuna and Llama 2. An orthogonal-shift regularizer raised Llama-3.2 ASR from 0.0145 to 0.0265 at coefficient 0.00001, a larger gain than the suffix-push regularizer.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Jailbreak suffix success also depends on activation changes outside the refusal direction, in a model-dependent way.

fits_no_version.finding: Prompt refusal connectivity (the prompt's projection on the direction) negatively predicts transfer in joint models for Qwen, Vicuna and Llama 2. Rephrasing changes in the dot product correlate negatively with ASR change (Qwen -0.08, Llama 3.2 -0.18).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Harmful prompts more aligned with the refusal direction are harder to jailbreak with transferred suffixes.

record.problems: The principal transfer-mechanism results are regression associations, not direct causal tests of refusal-direction suppression. The direction-regularized attack results report ASR but not the resulting activation shifts. No general-capability evaluation is reported.
record.rows_left_out: Rows r22-r27 are referenced under fits_no_version but not included in the main rows array: prompt-connectivity coefficients (Table 2) and prompt-rephrasing correlations (Section 5.6) do not measure attacks suppressing the refusal direction. Orthogonal-shift regression and regularized-attack results are also omitted from the main rows because they concern shifts perpendicular to the direction, not the V3 suppression claim.

untested.parts: The study does not causally test that the attack works through the direction (e.g., ablating or re-adding the direction under a suffix). It does not test training against direction ablation or the robustness that such training would add. It does not measure activation shifts under the regularized attack.
Ablation, addition and capability retention are not tested. The direction is only used as a measurement axis.

missing.what: Qualitative evidence that the most successful suffixes strongly suppress cosine similarity with the refusal direction across layers, while the least successful only marginally reduce it, in all four models.
Per-suffix plots showing ASR rising with suffix push for each model, with weaker signal for the Llama models.

record.verdict_notes: This is not an original source. The V3 support is correlational: suffix push is partly defined by the same projection used to judge harmfulness, and the paper never ablates the direction to show that attacks depend on it. All regularized-attack ASRs are under 3% on Llama-3.2-1B, with 20 prompts and no uncertainty reported. The orthogonal-shift results suggest attacks are not solely direction suppression, which is relevant to V3/V4 but not a direct test of V4.

versions.untested_parts: No causal ablation or addition of the difference-in-means direction; no evaluation of retained general capability.
No weight edit or abliteration evaluation.
The study tests suffix-push associations with transfer and a suffix-push-regularized attack, but does not test training against direction ablation or robustness after such training.
Orthogonal shifts are analyzed as predictors of transfer, but the study does not test whether refusal itself is affine, conical, or carried by multiple refusal directions.
No separate measurement or intervention on harmfulness judgment versus refusal decision.
Cross-model suffix transfer is studied, but transfer of the refusal direction across languages, variants, or base-to-instruct models is not tested.
No comparison of refusal-training methods or training stages for whether a removable direction emerges.

relationships.condition: Intra-model suffix transfer in Qwen-2.5-3B, Vicuna-13B, Llama-2-7B and Llama-3.2-1B, and Llama-3.2 to Qwen inter-model transfer
relationships.reason: Suffix push is a positive, significant predictor of transfer in the single-feature, joint and semantic-similarity-adjusted models (r1-r9, r11-r14). It is the largest main effect in all models except Vicuna. The evidence is correlational only.
relationships.display_finding: Suffix displacement positively and significantly predicted transfer in single-feature, joint and semantic-similarity-adjusted analyses, providing the largest main effect except in Vicuna without establishing causality.

source_check.label: limits_scope
source_check.reason: The suffix-push coefficient is -0.99 and non-significant. The authors blame the very low transfer success, so the test is underpowered. That makes it too weak for challenges, and limits_scope is the conservative label.

relationships.reason: Encouraging push raises ASR only modestly, and only at small coefficients (0.0138 to at most 0.0214). ASR drops at 0.1 and 0.5. The gain depends on the coefficient, and the achieved push is unreported (r15-r21).
relationships.display_finding: Small regularization coefficients increased attack success only from 0.0138 to at most 0.0214, while coefficients of 0.1 and 0.5 reduced success.

relation.reason: Its own results (Tables 2, 3, 4 and 8) bear on whether attacks succeed by pushing activations away from the refusal direction.

tranche.reason: It asks whether jailbreak suffixes work through suppressing the Arditi difference-in-means direction. It answers by regressing suffix transfer on suffix push across 4 models, plus a regularized-GCG intervention, not by ablation.

source_check.notes: The pack gave no [lN] verdict ids, so l1-l3 are assigned in listed order. Same study as arXiv:2510.22014, published in TMLR 05/2026 (year 2026, not '?'). r9 significance should be p<0.001. The second part of V3 (training against ablation adds robustness) is untested. The orthogonal-shift regularizer (Table 5) and the prompt-rephrasing intervention are not rows here.

statements.correction: 990,000 prompt-suffix observations per model (intra-model). Llama-3.2->Qwen suffix push 1.34 is p<0.001 (N = 9,900).
statements.problem: For this study the numbers are right: single-feature 1.28-3.56 and joint 1.06-3.61, both p<0.001, and Llama-3.2->Qwen 1.34. Minor point: 990,000 is the number of prompt-suffix pairs per model, not the total.
Accurate. The same study is cited elsewhere as arXiv:2510.22014; here it is cited by its OpenReview link.

reader_labels.condition: Intra-model transfer across Qwen, Vicuna, Llama 2, and Llama 3.2; also Llama 3.2 to Qwen
reader_labels.reason: Suffix push has a positive, statistically significant association with transfer success in the reported models and analysis specifications (r1-r9, r11-r14).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
